topicName: Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD) Types 1, 2, and 3 in ETL"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In Data Warehousing and ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipelines, dimensions store contextual data about business entities like customers, products, and employees. Often, this data changes over time. Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD) refer to the techniques used to manage and track these changes. Choosing the right SCD type is crucial for maintaining historical accuracy and reporting integrity."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Type 1 SCD: Overwrite"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Type 1 SCD involves simply overwriting the existing data in the dimension table with the new data. No historical record of the previous value is maintained. This approach is straightforward and saves storage space, but it results in the complete loss of historical context."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Easy to implement, requires minimal storage, no need to update historical fact tables."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Loss of historical data, impossible to run point-in-time historical reports based on the old attribute value."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"UPDATE dim_customer SET customer_address = '123 New St' WHERE customer_id = 1001;"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Type 2 SCD: Row Versioning"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Type 2 SCD is the most common approach for tracking history. When an attribute changes, a completely new row is inserted into the dimension table. This new row becomes the current record, and the old row is marked as expired. Metadata columns such as effective_start_date, effective_end_date, and is_current (or a version number) are typically used to manage this."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Preserves complete history, enables accurate point-in-time reporting."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Increases database storage, complicates ETL logic and surrogate key handling in fact tables."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"-- Step 1: Expire the current record
UPDATE dim_customer SET is_current = 0, effective_end_date = '2023-10-25' WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND is_current = 1;

-- Step 2: Insert the new active record
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_id, customer_address, effective_start_date, effective_end_date, is_current)
VALUES (1001, '456 Market St', '2023-10-26', '9999-12-31', 1);"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Type 3 SCD: Added Column"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Type 3 SCD tracks limited history by adding a new column to the dimension table to store the previous value alongside the current value. When a change occurs, the current value is moved to the previous column, and the new value overwrites the current column."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pros: Avoids the row explosion of Type 2, simpler to query than Type 2 for specific historical comparisons."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cons: Only tracks a fixed number of changes (usually just the immediately preceding value), schema changes are required if more history must be tracked."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"UPDATE dim_customer SET previous_address = customer_address, customer_address = '789 Broadway', address_change_date = '2023-10-26' WHERE customer_id = 1001;"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Best Practices"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"When designing your ETL pipeline, select Type 1 for correcting data entry errors or when history is strictly irrelevant. Choose Type 2 for compliance, auditing, and comprehensive business intelligence requirements. Reserve Type 3 for rare scenarios where tracking just the previous state is sufficient and row-level history adds unnecessary complexity."}]
